newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greek Cypriots clash with police over peace concert.
newsitem.headline: Greek Cypriots clash with police over peace concert.

text.p: Greek Cypriots opposed to a United Nations-sponsored peace concert in the no-man's land dividing the island battled riot police on Monday in the streets of Nicosia.

Greek Cypriot antagonism to the free concert -- for both Turkish and Greek Cypriots -- was underlined by a protest concert in the Greek half of the capital which attracted about 5,000 people -- some 1,000 more than the estimated audience at the peace concert.

On the Turkish side, witnesses reported far-right Turkish "Grey Wolf" nationalists threw stones at the bus carrying the Turkish singer to join a Greek pop star at the peace concert. Windows were broken but there were no injuries, they said.

About 200 protesters, including members of motorcycle clubs often involved in incidents along the line dividing the island, battled Greek Cypriot police in the business heart of their side of the capital.

Demonstrators smashed windows of police cars and threw at least two petrol bombs. Trash bins were set on fire and protesters lobbed stones at police -- a continuation of clashes that began before the concert with police protecting access to the concert site.
Police responded with tear gas. One policeman and one fireman were injured by stones, police said. They said they had arrested "scores" of people.
Police had mounted a massive security operation in the capital to ensure the concert remained peaceful. U.N. soldiers checked those entering and it passed off without incident.
Pop stars Burak Kut of Turkey and Sakis Rouvas of Greece sang for the crowd of young people in the U.N.-controlled no-man's land beside the Venetian walls that had once protected the city.
The aim was to break the ice, or begin to thaw it, between the youth of the island's two communities separated by years of enmity and mistrust.
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in an invasion sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
The concert took on a political meaning in the face of angry reactions from various groups on both sides of the divide.
A far-right Turkish nationalist group had driven around the Turkish section of Nicosia on Monday afternoon with loudspeakers publicising a protest meeting against the concert for the evening.
In the south, Greek Cypriot groups who saw the concert as an act of defeatism and Turkish propaganda announced their protest concert two km from the peace concert.
